EDITORIAL: Endorsement: Reject Props. 1 and 37: Californians can't borrow their way out of our housing crisis.
By East Bay Times
The Tribune Content Agency
October 26, 2026 5:49 PM
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...
The problem underlying California's housing crisis comes down to this: the cost of construction.
It constrains new supply. And the only way to recoup the costs of what does get built requires high rents and mortgages or - in the case of affordable housing - public subsidies.
Unfortunately, the solution to this crisis offered by two statewide propositions has nothing to do with addressing prohibitive building costs. Instead, their answer is to load Californians with debt while delivering bonanzas to home developers and builders.
Proposition 1 leaves taxpayers indebted; Proposition 37, homebuyers.
Reject both.
Proposition 1
This measure, placed on the ballot by the state Legislature through Senate Bill 407, is an expensive pandering potpourri of giveaways. Veterans, farmworkers, students, tribes are all the ostensible beneficiaries.
Here's how it is supposed to work:
Proposition 1 would authorize the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds, all earmarked for various housing programs. The bulk of the bonds, $7.2 billion, would be spent acquiring, building or renovating apartments. The backers of this proposition optimistically estimate that it would subsidize the construction of "up to" 40,000 multifamily rental units as well as 2,500 housing units for farmworkers and 1,200 beds for university students.
Another $1.1 billion would provide homeownership assistance for 40,000 families. The remainder of funds would go toward infrastructure projects ($500 million), farmworker housing ($450 million), student housing at the UC and Cal State systems ($350 million), and tribal housing ($200 million).
Additionally, $1.25 billion would be dedicated to home loan assistance for veterans. (This program is not expected to create direct costs as participating veterans would pay monthly payments to the state, according to the Legislative Analyst's Office.)
The need for affordable housing and housing assistance in this state is undeniable. More than two in five households spend, at least, 30% of their incomes on housing.
However, Proposition 1 would only provide a drop in the bucket towards adding to the state's housing supply, all while hamstringing state spending and burdening taxpayers with decades of debt. The LAO projects that paying off $10 billion in bond debt incurred by this measure would require annual payments between $500 million to $600 million for a quarter of a century. These payments would come from California's checking account, the General Fund. Because the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, per the LAO, the total cost of the bond would be about 15% more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
Perhaps that would be acceptable if this burst of spending would make a long-term difference, but it's doubtful.
Consider that California needs to build 2.5 million new homes, including 1 million affordable ones, to keep up with demand.
But this measure would add only 4% toward the affordable total, and that's only under pie-in-the-sky circumstances.
More disconcerting is how this measure would do nothing to attack the root of the affordable housing cost problem:
Building subsidized housing in California costs 1.5 times the average cost of building already-exorbitant market-rate housing here, according to a 2025 RAND study.
The nonpartisan think tank identified two major reasons for the discrepancy: Local governments charge "unusually large" architectural and engineering fees, and they require that affordable housing developers pay "substantially above-market" wages.
While $200 million of Proposition 1 would go toward "pilot" programs aimed at developing reduced housing models, at least $10 billion would be spent keeping this bloated model afloat.
Proposition 37
This measure looks great on the surface. It would help Californians buy new homes, all without costing taxpayers a dime.
Well, all that glitters isn't gold.
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for downpayment assistance on newly constructed homes. Eligible buyers could borrow up to 17% of a home's purchase price through a fixed-rate second mortgage, making a down payment as low as 3%.
For example, consider an $800,000 home. A buyer could put down $24,000, borrow $136,000 through Proposition 37 and then finance the remaining $640,000 using a conventional mortgage.
A 30-year loan at today's rates would make the monthly costs of that second mortgage more than $900.
Proposition 37 is not reducing the burden of home prices in California.
It's not solving the affordability crisis.
It's just a creative way to help Californians take on more debt.
What rightly worries critics is the terms of these additional loans. When borrowers default, the primary mortgage lender gets repaid first, meaning that the owner of the secondary takes on more risk. That would almost certainly mean that investors would require that buyers pay higher rates on their second mortgages than they pay on the first.
The LAO identifies these financing terms and investor participation as significant uncertainties.
Proposition 37 does nothing to address the main obstacle to homeownership in the state: the monthly cost of a conventional mortgage.
While the majority of renters in the state have incomes that would make them eligible to benefit from the measure's secondary mortgage program, many wouldn't qualify for a conventional mortgage in the first place even with its down payment assistance, according to the Public Policy Institute of California.
Far from solving the problem of high home prices, Proposition 37 could compound it.
While the measure restricts using the downpayment assistance to previously unpurchased homes, that does not mean that Proposition 37 will unleash a large new supply of housing.
What's infinitely more probable is that Proposition 37 would expand purchasing power faster than it would induce new construction - and therefore push up prices.
Homes in California, especially new ones, are sitting unsold longer. In fact, builders have created a glut of new housing in the Central Valley they can't sell, a dynamic exacerbated as interest rates have climbed. In fact, this summer Fresno topped Realtor.com (http://realtor.com/)'s list of U.S. cities with the highest share of new home listings (68%) cutting prices. Builders in the region, like Lennar, are reportedly panicking and responding by offering steeper discounts to lure buyers.
But Proposition 37 would give future builders an escape hatch, if not a bonanza. Instead of having to lower prices, it could artificially inflate the market by putting (borrowed) cash into buyers' hands.
No wonder realtors, carpenters and builders are throwing money to get this passed.
There is a role for government to play in California's housing crisis. But these two measures aren't it.
We can't solve our way out by pumping more money into a broken system and calling creative ways to finance more debt the solution.
Reject Propositions 1 and 37.

EDITORIAL: Endorsement: Reject Props. 1 and 37: Californians can't borrow their way out of our housing crisis.
By East Bay Times
The Tribune Content Agency
October 26, 2026 5:49 PM
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...
The problem underlying California's housing crisis comes down to this: the cost of construction.
It constrains new supply. And the only way to recoup the costs of what does get built requires high rents and mortgages or - in the case of affordable housing - public subsidies.
Unfortunately, the solution to this crisis offered by two statewide propositions has nothing to do with addressing prohibitive building costs. Instead, their answer is to load Californians with debt while delivering bonanzas to home developers and builders.
Proposition 1 leaves taxpayers indebted; Proposition 37, homebuyers.
Reject both.
Proposition 1
This measure, placed on the ballot by the state Legislature through Senate Bill 407, is an expensive pandering potpourri of giveaways. Veterans, farmworkers, students, tribes are all the ostensible beneficiaries.
Here's how it is supposed to work:
Proposition 1 would authorize the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds, all earmarked for various housing programs. The bulk of the bonds, $7.2 billion, would be spent acquiring, building or renovating apartments. The backers of this proposition optimistically estimate that it would subsidize the construction of "up to" 40,000 multifamily rental units as well as 2,500 housing units for farmworkers and 1,200 beds for university students.
Another $1.1 billion would provide homeownership assistance for 40,000 families. The remainder of funds would go toward infrastructure projects ($500 million), farmworker housing ($450 million), student housing at the UC and Cal State systems ($350 million), and tribal housing ($200 million).
Additionally, $1.25 billion would be dedicated to home loan assistance for veterans. (This program is not expected to create direct costs as participating veterans would pay monthly payments to the state, according to the Legislative Analyst's Office.)
The need for affordable housing and housing assistance in this state is undeniable. More than two in five households spend, at least, 30% of their incomes on housing.
However, Proposition 1 would only provide a drop in the bucket towards adding to the state's housing supply, all while hamstringing state spending and burdening taxpayers with decades of debt. The LAO projects that paying off $10 billion in bond debt incurred by this measure would require annual payments between $500 million to $600 million for a quarter of a century. These payments would come from California's checking account, the General Fund. Because the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, per the LAO, the total cost of the bond would be about 15% more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
Perhaps that would be acceptable if this burst of spending would make a long-term difference, but it's doubtful.
Consider that California needs to build 2.5 million new homes, including 1 million affordable ones, to keep up with demand.
But this measure would add only 4% toward the affordable total, and that's only under pie-in-the-sky circumstances.
More disconcerting is how this measure would do nothing to attack the root of the affordable housing cost problem:
Building subsidized housing in California costs 1.5 times the average cost of building already-exorbitant market-rate housing here, according to a 2025 RAND study.
The nonpartisan think tank identified two major reasons for the discrepancy: Local governments charge "unusually large" architectural and engineering fees, and they require that affordable housing developers pay "substantially above-market" wages.
While $200 million of Proposition 1 would go toward "pilot" programs aimed at developing reduced housing models, at least $10 billion would be spent keeping this bloated model afloat.
Proposition 37
This measure looks great on the surface. It would help Californians buy new homes, all without costing taxpayers a dime.
Well, all that glitters isn't gold.
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for downpayment assistance on newly constructed homes. Eligible buyers could borrow up to 17% of a home's purchase price through a fixed-rate second mortgage, making a down payment as low as 3%.
For example, consider an $800,000 home. A buyer could put down $24,000, borrow $136,000 through Proposition 37 and then finance the remaining $640,000 using a conventional mortgage.
A 30-year loan at today's rates would make the monthly costs of that second mortgage more than $900.
Proposition 37 is not reducing the burden of home prices in California.
It's not solving the affordability crisis.
It's just a creative way to help Californians take on more debt.
What rightly worries critics is the terms of these additional loans. When borrowers default, the primary mortgage lender gets repaid first, meaning that the owner of the secondary takes on more risk. That would almost certainly mean that investors would require that buyers pay higher rates on their second mortgages than they pay on the first.
The LAO identifies these financing terms and investor participation as significant uncertainties.
Proposition 37 does nothing to address the main obstacle to homeownership in the state: the monthly cost of a conventional mortgage.
While the majority of renters in the state have incomes that would make them eligible to benefit from the measure's secondary mortgage program, many wouldn't qualify for a conventional mortgage in the first place even with its down payment assistance, according to the Public Policy Institute of California.
Far from solving the problem of high home prices, Proposition 37 could compound it.
While the measure restricts using the downpayment assistance to previously unpurchased homes, that does not mean that Proposition 37 will unleash a large new supply of housing.
What's infinitely more probable is that Proposition 37 would expand purchasing power faster than it would induce new construction - and therefore push up prices.
Homes in California, especially new ones, are sitting unsold longer. In fact, builders have created a glut of new housing in the Central Valley they can't sell, a dynamic exacerbated as interest rates have climbed. In fact, this summer Fresno topped Realtor.com (http://realtor.com/)'s list of U.S. cities with the highest share of new home listings (68%) cutting prices. Builders in the region, like Lennar, are reportedly panicking and responding by offering steeper discounts to lure buyers.
But Proposition 37 would give future builders an escape hatch, if not a bonanza. Instead of having to lower prices, it could artificially inflate the market by putting (borrowed) cash into buyers' hands.
No wonder realtors, carpenters and builders are throwing money to get this passed.
There is a role for government to play in California's housing crisis. But these two measures aren't it.
We can't solve our way out by pumping more money into a broken system and calling creative ways to finance more debt the solution.
Reject Propositions 1 and 37.

They’d take out debt to pay for housing and medical research. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Your November ballot is welcoming you to make it rain … in bonds. You’ll see an El Nino-sized set of propositions that could flood the housing construction and science research components of the California economy with $44 billion of bond spending if the measures pass. Two of those bond proposals — Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) for housing and Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) for immunology research — are the traditional borrow-now, pay-back-later arrangements that add a few billion dollars to the overall cost of the propositions. A third, Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/), is an atypical measure that amounts to a low-risk radical experiment that taxpayers likely won’t be on the hook for, at least not directly. Historically, bond propositions win the approval of voters at higher rates than other measures. Since 2000, voters passed 23 of the 26 statewide bonds before them, an 88% yay rate. In recent years voters approved billions in bond debt for school construction, combatting the effects of climate change and housing for veterans. Bonds are a form of debt that the state must pay off over time, and that means annual payments with interest (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm). The state spends $6 billion annually to repay about $80 billion of bonds. Voters and lawmakers have also approved $40 billion in bonds that have yet to be sold. Fortunately for your ballot studying, the following cheat sheet is a primer on just the three bonds before you. Prop. 1: Affordable housing If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless. The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature. This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election. Opposition to this bond is minimal. The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure. Several Republican lawmakers in June voted no on the bill that metamorphosed into this bond. They argued that the bill’s title — The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) — misled the public on just how much of the bond revenue would support veterans. The answer? $1.25 billion for veterans to secure home loans. Another $350 million would head to the state’s two public university systems to help finance the development of student dorms. But with costs per bed often exceeding $250,000, all those tens of millions of dollars would secure dorms for around 1,300 students. Read CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall’s guide to Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/). Prop. 37: Help for down payments This bond measure is strange (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns. Confused? So is everyone else, which is why CalMatters’ housing reporter Ben Christopher described this unorthodox proposition as “plainly weird.” (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/) Prop. 37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments. The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome. That covers much of the typical 20% down payment. Who’s eligible? Roughly 90% of all California renters. The income caps vary by county, so around $115,000 in Imperial and north of $400,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. Eligible homes must satisfy several conditions: They’re new or newly converted and don’t cost more than roughly $1.5 million in the Bay Area or $1 million in Riverside — again, it’s based on a weedy formula by county. What won’t it do? Add to the state’s debt repayment log. This is not a bond that taxpayers will pay back; instead private lenders who provide this bond money will be repaid by homebuyers in the form of interest payments. How many homes this could buy is impossible to predict. That number depends on how much the new homes cost, the incomes of the homebuyers and whether developers build new homes. Most renters today couldn’t afford even the cheapest new homes, said Eric McGhee, an analyst for the nonprofit Public Policy Institute of California who’s written about Prop. 37 (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/). He estimated that anywhere from 60,000 to more than 1.8 million buyers could take advantage of the down payment assistance through this bond measure. The lower end assumes a 20% down payment on the most expensive homes. The higher end assumes 5% down payments on the least expensive homes. Prop. 38: Immunology research This bond proposal (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) would commit $4.2 billion to a single, unnamed nonprofit institute that focuses on immunology research and cures for major diseases such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The same amount would be distributed to a committee that’d identify a limited number of researchers at public universities and nonprofits who study immunology and immunotherapies. Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets Prop. 38’s criteria for half of the money: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign. Additional CalMatters reporting raises the question of how ready is the institute to implement the bond’s vast dollars. The institute had only three employees (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) as of last month, far fewer than the 51 it planned to have on staff last year. The Yes on 38 campaign says the bond revenue is needed to hedge against the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to cut federal science research or limit what’s studied. They argue that any curtailment of drug trials and other therapies can lead to avoidable pain and death for patients of debilitating maladies. Opponents of the measure fault it for concentrating half the money in a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the funding. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists. EDITORIAL: Endorsement: Reject Props. 1 and 37: Californians can't borrow their way out of our housing crisis.
By East Bay Times
The Tribune Content Agency
October 26, 2026 5:49 PM
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...
The problem underlying California's housing crisis comes down to this: the cost of construction.
It constrains new supply. And the only way to recoup the costs of what does get built requires high rents and mortgages or - in the case of affordable housing - public subsidies.
Unfortunately, the solution to this crisis offered by two statewide propositions has nothing to do with addressing prohibitive building costs. Instead, their answer is to load Californians with debt while delivering bonanzas to home developers and builders.
Proposition 1 leaves taxpayers indebted; Proposition 37, homebuyers.
Reject both.
Proposition 1
This measure, placed on the ballot by the state Legislature through Senate Bill 407, is an expensive pandering potpourri of giveaways. Veterans, farmworkers, students, tribes are all the ostensible beneficiaries.
Here's how it is supposed to work:
Proposition 1 would authorize the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds, all earmarked for various housing programs. The bulk of the bonds, $7.2 billion, would be spent acquiring, building or renovating apartments. The backers of this proposition optimistically estimate that it would subsidize the construction of "up to" 40,000 multifamily rental units as well as 2,500 housing units for farmworkers and 1,200 beds for university students.
Another $1.1 billion would provide homeownership assistance for 40,000 families. The remainder of funds would go toward infrastructure projects ($500 million), farmworker housing ($450 million), student housing at the UC and Cal State systems ($350 million), and tribal housing ($200 million).
Additionally, $1.25 billion would be dedicated to home loan assistance for veterans. (This program is not expected to create direct costs as participating veterans would pay monthly payments to the state, according to the Legislative Analyst's Office.)
The need for affordable housing and housing assistance in this state is undeniable. More than two in five households spend, at least, 30% of their incomes on housing.
However, Proposition 1 would only provide a drop in the bucket towards adding to the state's housing supply, all while hamstringing state spending and burdening taxpayers with decades of debt. The LAO projects that paying off $10 billion in bond debt incurred by this measure would require annual payments between $500 million to $600 million for a quarter of a century. These payments would come from California's checking account, the General Fund. Because the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, per the LAO, the total cost of the bond would be about 15% more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
Perhaps that would be acceptable if this burst of spending would make a long-term difference, but it's doubtful.
Consider that California needs to build 2.5 million new homes, including 1 million affordable ones, to keep up with demand.
But this measure would add only 4% toward the affordable total, and that's only under pie-in-the-sky circumstances.
More disconcerting is how this measure would do nothing to attack the root of the affordable housing cost problem:
Building subsidized housing in California costs 1.5 times the average cost of building already-exorbitant market-rate housing here, according to a 2025 RAND study.
The nonpartisan think tank identified two major reasons for the discrepancy: Local governments charge "unusually large" architectural and engineering fees, and they require that affordable housing developers pay "substantially above-market" wages.
While $200 million of Proposition 1 would go toward "pilot" programs aimed at developing reduced housing models, at least $10 billion would be spent keeping this bloated model afloat.
Proposition 37
This measure looks great on the surface. It would help Californians buy new homes, all without costing taxpayers a dime.
Well, all that glitters isn't gold.
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for downpayment assistance on newly constructed homes. Eligible buyers could borrow up to 17% of a home's purchase price through a fixed-rate second mortgage, making a down payment as low as 3%.
For example, consider an $800,000 home. A buyer could put down $24,000, borrow $136,000 through Proposition 37 and then finance the remaining $640,000 using a conventional mortgage.
A 30-year loan at today's rates would make the monthly costs of that second mortgage more than $900.
Proposition 37 is not reducing the burden of home prices in California.
It's not solving the affordability crisis.
It's just a creative way to help Californians take on more debt.
What rightly worries critics is the terms of these additional loans. When borrowers default, the primary mortgage lender gets repaid first, meaning that the owner of the secondary takes on more risk. That would almost certainly mean that investors would require that buyers pay higher rates on their second mortgages than they pay on the first.
The LAO identifies these financing terms and investor participation as significant uncertainties.
Proposition 37 does nothing to address the main obstacle to homeownership in the state: the monthly cost of a conventional mortgage.
While the majority of renters in the state have incomes that would make them eligible to benefit from the measure's secondary mortgage program, many wouldn't qualify for a conventional mortgage in the first place even with its down payment assistance, according to the Public Policy Institute of California.
Far from solving the problem of high home prices, Proposition 37 could compound it.
While the measure restricts using the downpayment assistance to previously unpurchased homes, that does not mean that Proposition 37 will unleash a large new supply of housing.
What's infinitely more probable is that Proposition 37 would expand purchasing power faster than it would induce new construction - and therefore push up prices.
Homes in California, especially new ones, are sitting unsold longer. In fact, builders have created a glut of new housing in the Central Valley they can't sell, a dynamic exacerbated as interest rates have climbed. In fact, this summer Fresno topped Realtor.com (http://realtor.com/)'s list of U.S. cities with the highest share of new home listings (68%) cutting prices. Builders in the region, like Lennar, are reportedly panicking and responding by offering steeper discounts to lure buyers.
But Proposition 37 would give future builders an escape hatch, if not a bonanza. Instead of having to lower prices, it could artificially inflate the market by putting (borrowed) cash into buyers' hands.
No wonder realtors, carpenters and builders are throwing money to get this passed.
There is a role for government to play in California's housing crisis. But these two measures aren't it.
We can't solve our way out by pumping more money into a broken system and calling creative ways to finance more debt the solution.
Reject Propositions 1 and 37.

Photo by Jules Hotz for CalMatters In summary Californians will decide on $44 billion in bonds when the vote on Propositions 1, 37 and 38. They’d take out debt to pay for housing and medical research. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Your November ballot is welcoming you to make it rain … in bonds. You’ll see an El Nino-sized set of propositions that could flood the housing construction and science research components of the California economy with $44 billion of bond spending if the measures pass. Two of those bond proposals — Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) for housing and Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) for immunology research — are the traditional borrow-now, pay-back-later arrangements that add a few billion dollars to the overall cost of the propositions. A third, Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/), is an atypical measure that amounts to a low-risk radical experiment that taxpayers likely won’t be on the hook for, at least not directly. Historically, bond propositions win the approval of voters at higher rates than other measures. Since 2000, voters passed 23 of the 26 statewide bonds before them, an 88% yay rate. In recent years voters approved billions in bond debt for school construction, combatting the effects of climate change and housing for veterans. Bonds are a form of debt that the state must pay off over time, and that means annual payments with interest (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm). The state spends $6 billion annually to repay about $80 billion of bonds. Voters and lawmakers have also approved $40 billion in bonds that have yet to be sold. Fortunately for your ballot studying, the following cheat sheet is a primer on just the three bonds before you. Prop. 1: Affordable housing If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless. The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature. This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election. Opposition to this bond is minimal. The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure. Several Republican lawmakers in June voted no on the bill that metamorphosed into this bond. They argued that the bill’s title — The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) — misled the public on just how much of the bond revenue would support veterans. The answer? $1.25 billion for veterans to secure home loans. Another $350 million would head to the state’s two public university systems to help finance the development of student dorms. But with costs per bed often exceeding $250,000, all those tens of millions of dollars would secure dorms for around 1,300 students. Read CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall’s guide to Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/). Prop. 37: Help for down payments This bond measure is strange (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns. Confused? So is everyone else, which is why CalMatters’ housing reporter Ben Christopher described this unorthodox proposition as “plainly weird.” (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/) Prop. 37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments. The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome. That covers much of the typical 20% down payment. Who’s eligible? Roughly 90% of all California renters. The income caps vary by county, so around $115,000 in Imperial and north of $400,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. Eligible homes must satisfy several conditions: They’re new or newly converted and don’t cost more than roughly $1.5 million in the Bay Area or $1 million in Riverside — again, it’s based on a weedy formula by county. What won’t it do? Add to the state’s debt repayment log. This is not a bond that taxpayers will pay back; instead private lenders who provide this bond money will be repaid by homebuyers in the form of interest payments. How many homes this could buy is impossible to predict. That number depends on how much the new homes cost, the incomes of the homebuyers and whether developers build new homes. Most renters today couldn’t afford even the cheapest new homes, said Eric McGhee, an analyst for the nonprofit Public Policy Institute of California who’s written about Prop. 37 (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/). He estimated that anywhere from 60,000 to more than 1.8 million buyers could take advantage of the down payment assistance through this bond measure. The lower end assumes a 20% down payment on the most expensive homes. The higher end assumes 5% down payments on the least expensive homes. Prop. 38: Immunology research This bond proposal (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) would commit $4.2 billion to a single, unnamed nonprofit institute that focuses on immunology research and cures for major diseases such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The same amount would be distributed to a committee that’d identify a limited number of researchers at public universities and nonprofits who study immunology and immunotherapies. Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets Prop. 38’s criteria for half of the money: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign. Additional CalMatters reporting raises the question of how ready is the institute to implement the bond’s vast dollars. The institute had only three employees (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) as of last month, far fewer than the 51 it planned to have on staff last year. The Yes on 38 campaign says the bond revenue is needed to hedge against the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to cut federal science research or limit what’s studied. They argue that any curtailment of drug trials and other therapies can lead to avoidable pain and death for patients of debilitating maladies. Opponents of the measure fault it for concentrating half the money in a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the funding. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists. # Proposition 1 – An Overview
## What is Proposition 1
Proposition 1 was passed by California voters in March 2024.
The two-bill package, Senate Bill (SB) 326 (Eggman, Chapter 790, Statutes of 2023) and Assembly Bill (AB) 531 (Irwin, Chapter 789, Statutes of 2023), proposed statewide efforts to reform and expand California’s behavioral health system, and was put on the ballot by the California State Legislature and the Governor.
...
Proposition 1 consists of two parts: The Behavioral Health Services Act and the Behavioral Health Bond.
## What is the Behavioral Health Services Act?
The Behavioral Health Services Act replaces the Mental Health Services Act of 2004.
It reforms behavioral health care funding to prioritize services for people with the most significant mental health needs while adding the treatment of substance use disorders (SUD), expanding housing interventions, and increasing the behavioral health workforce.
...
## What is the Behavioral Health Bond?
The Behavioral Health Bond authorizes $6.4 billion in bonds to finance behavioral health treatment beds, supportive housing, community sites, and funding for housing veterans with behavioral health needs:
- $4.4 billion of these funds will be administered by DHCS for grants to public and private entities for behavioral health treatment and residential settings.
- $1.5 billion of the $4.4 billion will be awarded only to counties, cities, and tribal entities, with $30 million set aside for tribes.
- The remaining $1.9

2. Proposition 1 Official Title and Summary
https://vigarchive.sos.ca.gov/2024/primary/propositions/1/title-summary.htm
## AUTHORIZES $6.38 BILLION IN BONDS TO BUILD MENTAL HEALTH TREATMENT FACILITIES FOR THOSE WITH MENTAL HEALTH AND SUBSTANCE USE CHALLENGES; PROVIDES HOUSING FOR THE HOMELESS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
...
### PREPARED BY THE ATTORNEY GENERAL
- Authorizes $6.38 billion in state general obligation bonds for mental health treatment facilities ($4.4 billion) and supportive housing for homeless veterans and homeless individuals with behavioral health challenges ($2 billion).
- Amends Mental Health Services Act to:
- - Allow funding to be used to treat substance use disorders (instead of only mental health disorders);
- Re-allocate funding for full-service treatment programs, other behavioral health services (e.g., early intervention), and housing programs;
- Require annual audits of programs.
...
### SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST'S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT:
- Shift roughly $140 million annually of existing tax revenue for mental health, drug, and alcohol treatment from counties to the state.
- Increased state costs to repay bonds of about $310 million annually for 30 years.
These bond funds would be used to build (1) more places where people can get mental health care and drug or alcohol treatment and (2) more housing for people with mental health, drug, or alcohol challenges.

**What you need to know:** Just four months after passage, Governor Newsom today announced the availability of up to $3.3 billion in competitive grant funding to develop a wide range of behavioral health treatment settings for Californians who most need care.
...
**Sacramento, California** – Today, Governor Gavin Newsom announced the release of up to **$3.3 billion** in competitive grant funding from Proposition 1 to expand the behavioral health continuum and provide appropriate care to individuals experiencing mental health conditions and substance use disorders — with a particular focus on people who are most seriously ill, vulnerable, or homeless.
Proposition 1 includes two parts: a $6.4 billion Behavioral Health Bond for treatment settings and housing with services, and historic reform of the Behavioral Health Services Act (BHSA) to focus on people with the most serious illnesses, substance disorders, and housing needs.
...
Per Proposition 1, 30% of county BHSA funds each year must be directed to housing supports for people with serious behavioral health needs, including allowable ongoing capital to build more housing options.

PROP
1
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR HOUSING AFFORDABILITY PROGRAMS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Public Sector Funds Some Home Building. In most years, about 100,000 houses and apartments are built in California. Most of these housing units are built entirely with private dollars. Some, however, receive financial help from federal, state, or local governments. In the case of housing funded by the state, the state government generally provides local governments, nonprofit organizations, and private developers with grants or low-cost loans to fund a portion of the housing units’ construction costs. Typically, housing built with these funds must be sold or rented to Californians with low incomes.
Bonds Are a Common Way for the State to Fund Home Building and Homeownership Programs. Over the past few decades, the state has used general obligation bonds to fund various housing programs. Bonds are a way the state borrows money to cover the up-front costs of a development and then repays the money plus interest over time. The last statewide general obligation bond for affordable housing was approved by voters in 2024, providing $2 billion to provide housing for veterans and other people with mental health or substance use challenges who are facing homelessness.
Home Loan Program for Veterans. The state’s veterans home loan program provides home loans to eligible veterans, including veterans who may not otherwise qualify for a home loan. Under the program, the state sells general obligation bonds to investors and uses the funds to provide loans to veterans to purchase homes. Participating veterans repay the cost of the bonds through their payments on their home loan. The last statewide general obligation bond for veterans home loans was approved by voters in 2018, which provided $1 billion for the program.
PROPOSAL
New General Obligation Bond for Housing. Proposition 1 allows the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing purposes. This amount consists of (1) a $10 billion bond for a variety of state housing programs that would be repaid by the General Fund and (2) a $1.25 billion bond that would be repaid by veterans’ payments on their home loans. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons. For more information on the state’s General Fund-supported bonds, please see “Overview of State Bond Debt” later in this guide.)
State Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides bond funding for various types of housing programs, which are summarized in Figure 1. The funds would be allocated over a number of years. The major categories of housing programs supported by the bond are:
Affordable Multifamily Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides $7.2 billion to acquire, build, or renovate rental housing, such as apartment buildings&#46 These programs generally provide local governments and private developers with low-interest loans to fund part of the project cost. In exchange, projects generally must reserve units for low-income households for a period of 55 years. Some of this funding would be used for supportive housing, which provides on-site service (such as mental health and substance use counseling) to certain residents.
Homeownership Programs. Proposition 1 provides $1.1 billion to support homeownership for low- and moderate-income households. Some of the funds would be used to provide homebuying assistance for first-time homebuyers through loans that generally do not have to be paid back until the home is sold or paid off. Other funds would be provided to nonprofit organizations and other entities for activities such as acquiring land to build homes for eligible low-income homebuyers and repairing existing homes owned by low-income households.
Infrastructure Programs. Proposition 1 provides $500 million for a variety of infrastructure projects to support affordable housing developments, such as water, sewage, parks, and transportation improvements.
Farmworker Housing Program. Proposition 1 provides $450 million in loans and grants to build or renovate housing for farmworkers. Program funds could be used for both rental and owner-occupied housing.
Higher Education Student Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides $350 million, split evenly between the University of California and California State University, for affordable student housing.
Tribal Housing Program. Proposition 1 provides $200 million in grants to tribes. Funds could be used for various housing-related purposes, including construction and repair of rental and owner-occupied housing.
Local Pilot Programs. Proposition 1 provides $200 million that would be available to cities, counties, and certain other entities for pilot projects aimed at developing housing at reduced costs.
Veterans Housing Program. Proposition 1 also provides $1.25 billion for home loan assistance to veterans. Veterans generally use these loans to purchase single-family residences, condominiums, farms, and mobile homes.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Cost to Repay the $10 Billion Bond for Housing Programs. The state General Fund cost to repay the bond would be $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years . The estimated annual cost would be about one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Since the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, the total cost of the bond would be about 15 percent more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
No Direct State Cost for Veterans Housing Program. Veterans participating in the home loan program would make monthly payments to the state, allowing the state to repay the bonds. These payments have always covered the amount owed on the bonds, meaning the program has always operated at no direct cost to the state.
Administrative Costs. A number of state entities would experience increased costs to administer the various housing programs. A portion of the bond funds would cover these costs.
Impact of Funds. Much of the funding from Proposition 1 would be used together with other government monies to provide housing assistance. The bond funds would provide subsidies for up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, as well as about 2,500 units for farmworkers and about 1,200 beds for university students. The funds also would help up to 40,000 households, including about 2,100 veterans, with homeownership by providing homebuyer assistance and supporting the production and repair of homes.

ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 1
YES ON PROP. 1: AFFORDABLE HOMES FOR VETERANS, SENIORS, PEOPLE WITH DISABILITIES AND WORKING FAMILIES-WITHOUT RAISING TAXES
All Californians deserve a safe and affordable place to call home, but California has a housing shortage that is driving the nation’s worst housing affordability crisis. More than half of renters spend over 30% of their income on rent and only 22% of households can afford a median-priced home, yet only 1% of California’s state budget goes to housing.
Prop. 1 gives Californians the opportunity to:
Fast-track housing production;
Provide housing to working families, veterans, people with disabilities and seniors;
Help prevent homelessness by keeping our most vulnerable neighbors in their homes;
Expands homeownership opportunities;
Maintains strict fiscal accountability and transparency with NO NEW TAXES.
PROP. 1 HONORS OUR VETERANS
Dedicates $1.25 billion solely to veterans’ housing and homeownership opportunities through the existing CalVet Home Loan Program, which has already helped almost a million veterans and their families.
“California has one of the largest populations of homeless veterans in the nation. After their service, our veterans deserve a place to call home. Prop. 1 delivers on that promise.”-Michael Blecker, President, CA Association of Veteran Service Agencies
PROP. 1 BUILDS HOMES LOW- AND MIDDLE-INCOME FAMILIES CAN AFFORD
Prop. 1 jumpstarts the construction of tens of thousands of shovel-ready affordable homes across California, quickly turning stalled construction into move-in ready homes. The teacher in your child’s classroom, the firefighter who protects your neighborhood, first-time homebuyers, low- and middle-income Californians, and the nurse at your local hospital can no longer afford to live in most California communities. Prop. 1 builds more homes working people can actually afford.
NO NEW TAXES-STRICT ACCOUNTABILITY AND TRANSPARENCY
Prop. 1 doesn’t raise taxes and every dollar comes with strict accountability and public reporting. Voters will be able to see exactly how many homes get built, where, and at what cost. Prop. 1 unlocks federal matching funds, bringing tax dollars we send to Washington back home to California.
PROP. 1 HELPS SENIORS, VETERANS & OUR MOST VULNERABLE
Prop. 1 creates and preserves housing to help those who are one crisis away from homelessness stay off the streets, low-income seniors on fixed incomes, survivors of domestic violence and their families, veterans, at risk and foster youth, and people with disabilities who all deserve safe and stable homes.
PROP. 1 INVESTS IN COMMUNITIES & ESSENTIAL WORKERS
Quality, affordable housing is the foundation of thriving communities. Prop. 1 strengthens that foundation by helping essential workers-from firefighters and teachers to nurses-afford to live in the communities they serve. Working families and essential workers across California are being priced out and left behind. Prop. 1 enables the construction of affordable housing for these essential workers who dedicate their lives to our communities.
YES ON PROP. 1: SUPPORTED BY VETERANS, SENIORS, TEACHERS, FIREFIGHTERS, AND AFFORDABLE HOUSING ADVOCATES including Habitat for Humanity California, California Alliance for Retired Americans, Housing California, California Housing Consortium, California Alliance of Child and Family Services.
VOTE YES ON PROP. 1, Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond, to honor those veterans who served; provide safe and stable housing to California’s most vulnerable; guarantee strict fiscal accountability with no new taxes; and build the affordable homes all Californians deserve.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> Voters will decide on proposals to tax billionaires, extend taxes on high earners, fund biomedical research and more on the November general election ballot (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-general-election-voter-guide). Here’s everything you need to know about all the California propositions:
Proposition 1
The basics
Proposition 1 asks voters to let the state borrow $11.25 billion through the sale of bonds to build and maintain housing that low- and middle-income residents can afford. It’s called the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 1: Borrowing money for low-income and veteran housing (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-1-affordable-housing-voter-guide)
Prop 1 guide: Lawmakers are asking voters to let the state borrow $11.25 billion to build and maintain housing low- and middle-income residents can afford.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
The largest chunk of this money — $7.2 billion — would be doled out as loans to builders who agree to rent some of the homes to low-income families; in Los Angeles County, a family of four earning about $133,000 a year qualifies as low-income. Researchers recently found (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/sites/default/files/2026-03/2026_State_Pipeline_Brief.pdf) that the construction of nearly 40,000 low-income homes was in limbo because of a lack of funding.
Advertisement
The second-largest portion of these funds — $1.25 billion — would be set aside for housing for veterans, in the form of homeownership loans. Voters last approved this type of statewide bond for veteran home loans in 2018.
Dig deeper
Proposition 1 is supported by Democrats and organizations that provide low-income housing, plus various municipal governments. They say it is key to helping more Californians achieve homeownership. Republicans oppose it, saying the state should curtail building regulations to bring down the cost of housing without burdening taxpayers.
Proposition 2
The basics
Proposition 2 would give government the ability to put more money into savings and create another option for leaders to avoid triggering taxpayer rebates during future budget surpluses.
Advertisement
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 2: Lets leaders fatten ‘rainy day’ fund, reduces likelihood of taxpayer rebates (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-2-rainy-day-fund-voter-guide)
Prop 2 guide: California Democrats want to change the state constitution to allow them to deposit more money into budget reserves, creating another option to avoid giving excess revenue back to taxpayers.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
The measure exempts deposits into state savings accounts from a spending limit that voters previously adopted through a series of ballot measures dating to the late 1970s, and increases the share of general fund tax revenue that can be put aside in reserves.
Dig deeper
Democrats say the changes will allow the state to save more when the economy is growing and use the funds to lessen cuts to vital programs during bad times. Republicans say it will allow the state to spend more money that otherwise would go back to taxpayers.
Proposition 3
The basics
There has been much debate about efforts in California to tax the rich. But almost all of it centers around Proposition 40, (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) the heavily contested billionaire tax, and two countermeasures, Propositions 41 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide) and 42. (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-42-tax-ban-retirement-savings-voter-guide)
But Proposition 3 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide) — getting far less attention — also would tax California’s wealthiest citizens and has even garnered support from some billionaires who oppose Proposition 40. The proposition would make permanent an expiring state income tax on high earners.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 3: Making a high-income tax extension permanent (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide)
Prop 3 would make permanent an expiring income tax on the top 2% of California taxpayers that provides money for education, healthcare and other services.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
Tax rates for the top 2% of earners would remain as they are. Income brackets rise with inflation, but last year the top 2% of taxpayers earned at least $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers. Money generated by Proposition 3, like the current tax, would flow to education, with 89% going to K-12 schools and 11% to community colleges.
Dig deeper
In 2012, California voters approved a temporary increase in the income tax rate for the top 2% of California earners. In 2016, voters approved another extension through 2030. Proposition 3 would make the additional levy permanent.
Advertisement
Backers say the measure is crucial to maintain education funding levels and predict there would be grave problems if the measure is not approved.
The state could expect to lose from $5 billion to $15 billion annually in tax revenue starting in 2031, according to estimates from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Opponents say taxes are already too high and the state should focus on cutting waste.

EDITORIAL: Endorsement: Reject Props. 1 and 37: Californians can't borrow their way out of our housing crisis.
By East Bay Times
The Tribune Content Agency
October 26, 2026 5:49 PM
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...
The problem underlying California's housing crisis comes down to this: the cost of construction.
It constrains new supply. And the only way to recoup the costs of what does get built requires high rents and mortgages or - in the case of affordable housing - public subsidies.
Unfortunately, the solution to this crisis offered by two statewide propositions has nothing to do with addressing prohibitive building costs. Instead, their answer is to load Californians with debt while delivering bonanzas to home developers and builders.
Proposition 1 leaves taxpayers indebted; Proposition 37, homebuyers.
Reject both.
Proposition 1
This measure, placed on the ballot by the state Legislature through Senate Bill 407, is an expensive pandering potpourri of giveaways. Veterans, farmworkers, students, tribes are all the ostensible beneficiaries.
Here's how it is supposed to work:
Proposition 1 would authorize the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds, all earmarked for various housing programs. The bulk of the bonds, $7.2 billion, would be spent acquiring, building or renovating apartments. The backers of this proposition optimistically estimate that it would subsidize the construction of "up to" 40,000 multifamily rental units as well as 2,500 housing units for farmworkers and 1,200 beds for university students.
Another $1.1 billion would provide homeownership assistance for 40,000 families. The remainder of funds would go toward infrastructure projects ($500 million), farmworker housing ($450 million), student housing at the UC and Cal State systems ($350 million), and tribal housing ($200 million).
Additionally, $1.25 billion would be dedicated to home loan assistance for veterans. (This program is not expected to create direct costs as participating veterans would pay monthly payments to the state, according to the Legislative Analyst's Office.)
The need for affordable housing and housing assistance in this state is undeniable. More than two in five households spend, at least, 30% of their incomes on housing.
However, Proposition 1 would only provide a drop in the bucket towards adding to the state's housing supply, all while hamstringing state spending and burdening taxpayers with decades of debt. The LAO projects that paying off $10 billion in bond debt incurred by this measure would require annual payments between $500 million to $600 million for a quarter of a century. These payments would come from California's checking account, the General Fund. Because the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, per the LAO, the total cost of the bond would be about 15% more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
Perhaps that would be acceptable if this burst of spending would make a long-term difference, but it's doubtful.
Consider that California needs to build 2.5 million new homes, including 1 million affordable ones, to keep up with demand.
But this measure would add only 4% toward the affordable total, and that's only under pie-in-the-sky circumstances.
More disconcerting is how this measure would do nothing to attack the root of the affordable housing cost problem:
Building subsidized housing in California costs 1.5 times the average cost of building already-exorbitant market-rate housing here, according to a 2025 RAND study.
The nonpartisan think tank identified two major reasons for the discrepancy: Local governments charge "unusually large" architectural and engineering fees, and they require that affordable housing developers pay "substantially above-market" wages.
While $200 million of Proposition 1 would go toward "pilot" programs aimed at developing reduced housing models, at least $10 billion would be spent keeping this bloated model afloat.
Proposition 37
This measure looks great on the surface. It would help Californians buy new homes, all without costing taxpayers a dime.
Well, all that glitters isn't gold.
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for downpayment assistance on newly constructed homes. Eligible buyers could borrow up to 17% of a home's purchase price through a fixed-rate second mortgage, making a down payment as low as 3%.
For example, consider an $800,000 home. A buyer could put down $24,000, borrow $136,000 through Proposition 37 and then finance the remaining $640,000 using a conventional mortgage.
A 30-year loan at today's rates would make the monthly costs of that second mortgage more than $900.
Proposition 37 is not reducing the burden of home prices in California.
It's not solving the affordability crisis.
It's just a creative way to help Californians take on more debt.
What rightly worries critics is the terms of these additional loans. When borrowers default, the primary mortgage lender gets repaid first, meaning that the owner of the secondary takes on more risk. That would almost certainly mean that investors would require that buyers pay higher rates on their second mortgages than they pay on the first.
The LAO identifies these financing terms and investor participation as significant uncertainties.
Proposition 37 does nothing to address the main obstacle to homeownership in the state: the monthly cost of a conventional mortgage.
While the majority of renters in the state have incomes that would make them eligible to benefit from the measure's secondary mortgage program, many wouldn't qualify for a conventional mortgage in the first place even with its down payment assistance, according to the Public Policy Institute of California.
Far from solving the problem of high home prices, Proposition 37 could compound it.
While the measure restricts using the downpayment assistance to previously unpurchased homes, that does not mean that Proposition 37 will unleash a large new supply of housing.
What's infinitely more probable is that Proposition 37 would expand purchasing power faster than it would induce new construction - and therefore push up prices.
Homes in California, especially new ones, are sitting unsold longer. In fact, builders have created a glut of new housing in the Central Valley they can't sell, a dynamic exacerbated as interest rates have climbed. In fact, this summer Fresno topped Realtor.com (http://realtor.com/)'s list of U.S. cities with the highest share of new home listings (68%) cutting prices. Builders in the region, like Lennar, are reportedly panicking and responding by offering steeper discounts to lure buyers.
But Proposition 37 would give future builders an escape hatch, if not a bonanza. Instead of having to lower prices, it could artificially inflate the market by putting (borrowed) cash into buyers' hands.
No wonder realtors, carpenters and builders are throwing money to get this passed.
There is a role for government to play in California's housing crisis. But these two measures aren't it.
We can't solve our way out by pumping more money into a broken system and calling creative ways to finance more debt the solution.
Reject Propositions 1 and 37.

Photo by Jules Hotz for CalMatters In summary Californians will decide on $44 billion in bonds when the vote on Propositions 1, 37 and 38. They’d take out debt to pay for housing and medical research. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Your November ballot is welcoming you to make it rain … in bonds. You’ll see an El Nino-sized set of propositions that could flood the housing construction and science research components of the California economy with $44 billion of bond spending if the measures pass. Two of those bond proposals — Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) for housing and Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) for immunology research — are the traditional borrow-now, pay-back-later arrangements that add a few billion dollars to the overall cost of the propositions. A third, Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/), is an atypical measure that amounts to a low-risk radical experiment that taxpayers likely won’t be on the hook for, at least not directly. Historically, bond propositions win the approval of voters at higher rates than other measures. Since 2000, voters passed 23 of the 26 statewide bonds before them, an 88% yay rate. In recent years voters approved billions in bond debt for school construction, combatting the effects of climate change and housing for veterans. Bonds are a form of debt that the state must pay off over time, and that means annual payments with interest (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm). The state spends $6 billion annually to repay about $80 billion of bonds. Voters and lawmakers have also approved $40 billion in bonds that have yet to be sold. Fortunately for your ballot studying, the following cheat sheet is a primer on just the three bonds before you. Prop. 1: Affordable housing If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless. The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature. This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election. Opposition to this bond is minimal. The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure. Several Republican lawmakers in June voted no on the bill that metamorphosed into this bond. They argued that the bill’s title — The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) — misled the public on just how much of the bond revenue would support veterans. The answer? $1.25 billion for veterans to secure home loans. Another $350 million would head to the state’s two public university systems to help finance the development of student dorms. But with costs per bed often exceeding $250,000, all those tens of millions of dollars would secure dorms for around 1,300 students. Read CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall’s guide to Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/). Prop. 37: Help for down payments This bond measure is strange (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns. Confused? So is everyone else, which is why CalMatters’ housing reporter Ben Christopher described this unorthodox proposition as “plainly weird.” (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/) Prop. 37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments. The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome. That covers much of the typical 20% down payment. Who’s eligible? Roughly 90% of all California renters. The income caps vary by county, so around $115,000 in Imperial and north of $400,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. Eligible homes must satisfy several conditions: They’re new or newly converted and don’t cost more than roughly $1.5 million in the Bay Area or $1 million in Riverside — again, it’s based on a weedy formula by county. What won’t it do? Add to the state’s debt repayment log. This is not a bond that taxpayers will pay back; instead private lenders who provide this bond money will be repaid by homebuyers in the form of interest payments. How many homes this could buy is impossible to predict. That number depends on how much the new homes cost, the incomes of the homebuyers and whether developers build new homes. Most renters today couldn’t afford even the cheapest new homes, said Eric McGhee, an analyst for the nonprofit Public Policy Institute of California who’s written about Prop. 37 (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/). He estimated that anywhere from 60,000 to more than 1.8 million buyers could take advantage of the down payment assistance through this bond measure. The lower end assumes a 20% down payment on the most expensive homes. The higher end assumes 5% down payments on the least expensive homes. Prop. 38: Immunology research This bond proposal (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) would commit $4.2 billion to a single, unnamed nonprofit institute that focuses on immunology research and cures for major diseases such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The same amount would be distributed to a committee that’d identify a limited number of researchers at public universities and nonprofits who study immunology and immunotherapies. Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets Prop. 38’s criteria for half of the money: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign. Additional CalMatters reporting raises the question of how ready is the institute to implement the bond’s vast dollars. The institute had only three employees (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) as of last month, far fewer than the 51 it planned to have on staff last year. The Yes on 38 campaign says the bond revenue is needed to hedge against the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to cut federal science research or limit what’s studied. They argue that any curtailment of drug trials and other therapies can lead to avoidable pain and death for patients of debilitating maladies. Opponents of the measure fault it for concentrating half the money in a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the funding. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists. **Yes.**

*Why (briefly):* This Prop 1 (Nov. 2026, the $11.25B Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond) addresses a documented gap — nearly 40,000 affordable units are permitted and partially financed but stalled for lack of state subsidy, and each state dollar leverages roughly $3.60 in federal, local, and private funds. The repayment cost ($500–600M/year, ~0.25% of the General Fund) is modest for the scale of the problem, the veterans' portion is self-repaying, and even the state Republican Party is neutral with literally zero dollars raised against it — no official opposition argument was even submitted. The main criticisms (it adds debt without fixing construction-cost root causes) are real but don't outweigh getting shovel-ready homes built in a state with 180,000+ homeless residents.
